prize_parts.citation: For discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and its development into long-acting incretin therapies for type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: The round-1 exchange sharpened my view and did not overturn it. All six of us agree on the scientific core of B035: proglucagon processing, the insulinotropic action of the truncated active peptide, receptor biology and degradation-resistant agonists, now confirmed by independent outcome trials in glycaemia, weight, and cardiovascular and renal disease. No one disputes maturity. The only open question is what three names best represent that chain. I keep Drucker, Holst and Knudsen: Holst for human physiology of GLP-1 secretion and action, Drucker for receptor biology and the wider proglucagon-peptide axis, and Knudsen for the albumin-binding analogue design (liraglutide, semaglutide) that turned a hormone with a minutes-long half-life into a medicine. A Physiology or Medicine prize that carries physiology into patients should have a name on each stage, and the cap lets the credited list span physiology, receptor mechanism and translation. I keep a single-part prize, because no second part fits under three people without cutting a GLP-1 laureate, and I will not trade a name on the strongest candidate for a weaker one.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection to my configuration remains attribution, and I accept it fully. Five colleagues name Mojsov, and her identification and synthesis of the active GLP-1(7-36) form is a real contribution that my trio leaves out; Habener-era work is also outside the credited names. A prize that credits a drug developer and omits a peptide-identity contributor can be criticised as unfair to discovery, and the incretin story carries a commercial character that may read as confirmation of success more than selective judgment. I cannot verify the Mojsov priority record from the supplied material, and neither can the colleagues who rely on it, which cuts both ways: it is a reason not to rest a seat on a disputed claim, but equally not a reason to dismiss her. If the committee settles on a discovery-side trio, I would not regard that as a scientific error, only as a different weighting of the same chain.

responses.point: El-Manira would rather build the prize around the discovery of the hormone and its active form than around a single product, and names Mojsov, while acknowledging that either trio omits someone decisive (Knudsen if discovery is honoured, a discovery figure if development is).
responses.response: I agree with his framing of the dilemma and with his worry that a prize seen as unfair on credit would damage a very strong case. Where we differ is on which omission is easier to defend. The active-form priority is contested and none of us can verify it from the files, while Knudsen's role in designing the long-acting analogues is documented and is what made the physiology matter clinically. His 'active form' citation also carries a priority claim into the text of the prize itself, which I would rather avoid. My citation names the physiology and the development step without asserting who first identified the active peptide, and I think that wording is the one most defensible whichever third name is chosen.

responses.point: Sandberg frames the trio as honouring the discovery side, which she says is what a Physiology or Medicine prize is best placed to credit, and concedes that if the committee intends to recognise the drugs themselves her trio is the wrong trio.
responses.response: That concession is the crux, and I take it seriously. I read the remit differently: the incretin story is unusual because the physiology and the therapy are one continuous arc, and the largest outcome data come from the long-acting analogues, so I do not think a prize can credit the discovery side only and still describe why it matters. A prize for the 'idea' with Holst and Drucker already covers discovery of the biology; the third seat is the only place to represent translation, and I would use it there. I accept her point that Mojsov's work on the active form is not trivial, but I do not think leaving it out is more unfair than leaving out the person who delivered the clinical effect.

responses.point: Linnarsson says that leaving out Knudsen risks a prize that overlooks the person who delivered the clinical effect, and that if attribution problems prove unresolvable a cleaner candidate such as B028 with a two-person credit becomes more attractive.
responses.response: His own caveat supports my choice, since he accepts that the Knudsen omission is the main cost of his trio. On B028 I agree that attribution is cleaner and that the clinical effect in spinal muscular atrophy is documented, and I keep it as an alternative. But B035 is stronger on breadth of evidence and on the scale of patient benefit, and an unresolved third seat is a reason to resolve it, not to abandon the best candidate. A two-part prize of Drucker, Holst and a B028 laureate would cut Knudsen and Mojsov alike, and I do not think a cleaner credit justifies dropping a name from the stronger science.

responses.point: Svenningsson, as chair, keeps Mojsov and asks whether a second achievement such as the unfolded protein response (B047) could share the prize without cutting a GLP-1 laureate under the three-person limit.
responses.response: On the arithmetic it cannot: B047 has two names, so any two-part prize would reduce B035 to one person, which would break the physiology-to-therapy chain that makes the case. I therefore do not favour a second part this year. I repeat that I do not doubt the science of B047 and would regard it as a serious later-year candidate, with clean attribution and a clear mechanism, but its clinical consequence is still largely indirect, and I would not displace a GLP-1 laureate for it. I also agree with his point that Habener-type contributions are a fairness cost for any B035 trio, and I think it is better to name that cost than to pretend one trio avoids it.

responses.point: Perlmann prefers a single-achievement prize attached to a discovery rather than a product, and says he cannot resolve the priority dispute on the evidence in the files.
responses.response: We agree on the single-achievement structure and on the fact that neither of us can resolve the priority record from the files. Given that, I would not let an unverified priority claim decide the third seat. His worry that a physiology-only prize underweights the drug-development step that actually produced the benefit is the same one I have, and it is why I name the development leg in the citation.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will take Knudsen or Mojsov for the third seat; I cannot verify the Mojsov priority record, and five colleagues weigh it differently from me.

Whether a citation can be worded to be fair to both a development-inclusive and a discovery-only trio; my wording avoids stating who first identified the active peptide, but it may still be read as favouring development.
How much the absence of Habener-type contributions should count against any B035 trio; I treat it as an unavoidable cost of the three-person cap.

Whether a second part (B014, B028) would be better than one under the cap; I judge it not possible without cutting a GLP-1 laureate, and for B014 the Eshhar-type concept work lies outside the credited names.
My knowledge of incretin and other priority histories is general recollection, not verified from sources.
statement.conflict_note: No change from round 1. No specific conflict is apparent from my profile. My recorded co-authors (Vijay Kuchroo, Sven-Erik Sonesson) and my Bergen affiliation do not correspond to any credited name on the shortlisted candidates (B035, B014, B028); I am a rheumatology and autoimmunity researcher, which gives expertise but no personal tie. I have read the other members' disclosures and none involves a credited name on B035.
